rule: popup is the hover text, at most 240 characters; definition is the glossary-page text; every entry carries a source. side is market, lender or both; kind is series-id, acronym, instrument, metric, market or regulation; aliases are variants the page prints that resolve to the same entry. workingRef points maintainers at the design document and is never built or shown. The hover fields are built into frontend/lib/credit-terms.js by scripts/build-credit-terms.mjs; the Glossary view reads this file for the definitions.

terms.expansion: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread
terms.popup: High-yield bond spread. How much extra yield, over Treasuries, investors demand to hold US junk bonds. Under 3 points is tight; over 5 is stress.
terms.definition: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. The market-cap-weighted OAS of US-dollar, below-investment-grade (BB or lower) corporate bonds publicly issued in the US, measured against a spot Treasury curve. Daily close, percent. FRED serves only three years of history from April 2026, so the tile's percentile is a three-year window with a hand-keyed long-run anchor (2000-2026 median 457 bps, PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives figure 94).
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A0HYM2, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figure 94)
terms.whereUsed: Conditions strip tile 'High-yield OAS'; chart M1 spread ladder (HY bar)

terms.expansion: ICE BofA US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread
terms.popup: Investment-grade bond spread. The extra yield over Treasuries on bonds rated BBB or better. It is the calmest corner of credit; when it moves, everything else is moving more.
terms.definition: ICE BofA US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread. The market-cap-weighted OAS of US-dollar investment-grade (BBB or better) corporate bonds publicly issued in the US, against a spot Treasury curve; minimum $250 million outstanding, more than one year to maturity. Daily, percent, three years of history on FRED.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLC0A0CM, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: ICE BofA BB US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread
terms.popup: Spread on BB-rated bonds, the best-quality junk. The top rung of the high-yield ladder; the gap between this and CCC shows how far the market separates good and bad borrowers.
terms.definition: ICE BofA BB US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. OAS of the BB-rated subset of the ICE BofA US High Yield Master II Index, market-cap weighted, against a spot Treasury curve. Daily, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A1HYBB, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'BB / B / CCC OAS'; M1 ladder

terms.expansion: ICE BofA Single-B US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread
terms.popup: Spread on single-B bonds. The middle of the junk-bond ladder and the closest public match to a typical private-credit borrower, which is usually rated B or not rated at all.
terms.definition: ICE BofA Single-B US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. OAS of the B-rated subset of the ICE BofA US High Yield Master II Index, market-cap weighted, against a spot Treasury curve. Daily, percent. The spread ladder compares it with LCD's new-issue direct-lending LBO spread once the deck ingest lands.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A2HYB, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'BB / B / CCC OAS'; M1 ladder and its caption

terms.expansion: ICE BofA CCC & Lower US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread
terms.popup: Spread on CCC and lower bonds, the riskiest rated debt. It jumps first and furthest in a downturn, so its distance from BB is the market's fear gauge.
terms.definition: ICE BofA CCC & Lower US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. OAS of the CCC-and-below subset of the ICE BofA US High Yield Master II Index, market-cap weighted, against a spot Treasury curve. Daily, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A3HYC, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'BB / B / CCC OAS'; M1 ladder; the CCC-BB gap is the dispersion reading

terms.expansion: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Effective Yield
terms.popup: The all-in yield on US junk bonds, not just the spread. This is what a liquid, tradeable alternative to a private loan pays today.
terms.definition: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Effective Yield. The yield of the US-dollar below-investment-grade corporate bond index (constituents capitalization-weighted), which combines the Treasury rate and the credit spread. Daily, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A0HYM2EY, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'High-yield effective yield'; chart M2 yield stack

terms.popup: The overnight rate banks pay to borrow cash against Treasuries. It is the base rate for almost every floating-rate loan, so when SOFR moves, every borrower's interest bill moves with it.
terms.definition: Secured Overnight Financing Rate. The New York Fed's broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by Treasury securities, built from tri-party repo, GCF repo and FICC-cleared bilateral repo trades. Published each business day, percent. FRED history starts 2018-04-03, so the tile says 'since 2018'.
terms.source: New York Fed SOFR page https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/reference-rates/sofr (fetched 2026-09-11); the FRED page for SOFR carries no notes; history start from the FRED series page
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'SOFR and its 90-day average'; M2 yield stack; every 'spread over base' calculation

terms.popup: A three-month-style base rate that stands in for the term SOFR most loans reset off, which FRED does not carry. Used here to back the spread out of LCD's all-in rate.
terms.definition: 90-Day Average SOFR. The compounded average of SOFR over a rolling 90-day period, published by the New York Fed with the SOFR Averages and Index. Daily, percent. FRED history starts 2018-07-02. This site uses it (3.63% at Jun 30 2026) to back the BDC spread out of LCD's 8.30% all-in yield.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SOFR90DAYAVG, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'SOFR and its 90-day average'; section 4.4 spread-over-base check
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.expansion: Moody's Baa Corporate Bond Yield minus 10-Year Treasury
terms.popup: The gap between yields on Baa-rated corporate bonds and the 10-year Treasury. A long-run measure of how much extra the market charges a decent, not great, company to borrow.
terms.definition: Moody's Seasoned Baa Corporate Bond Yield Relative to Yield on 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity. Computed by the St. Louis Fed as Moody's Baa yield (DBAA) minus the 10-year constant-maturity Treasury yield. Daily, percent, history from 1986, so it carries the ten-year percentile and the long-run spread chart.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAA10Y, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: SLOOS net tightening, C&I, large and middle-market firms
terms.popup: Share of banks tightening loan terms for big and mid-sized companies, net of those loosening. Above 20 means banks are pulling back; that is when private lenders win business.
terms.definition: Net Percentage of Domestic Banks Tightening Standards for Commercial and Industrial Loans to Large and Middle-Market Firms, from the Fed's Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS). Quarterly, percent, history from 1990. Reading rule on the tile: over 20 tightening, under -10 loosening; the 2022-23 'banks retreat' regime.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DRTSCILM, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Tile 'Bank lending standards'; chart M3 bank standards vs private credit growth

terms.expansion: SLOOS net tightening, C&I, small firms
terms.popup: Same survey, but for loans to small companies. Small firms feel a bank pullback first, so this often leads the large-firm reading.
terms.definition: Net Percentage of Domestic Banks Tightening Standards for Commercial and Industrial Loans to Small Firms, from the SLOOS. Quarterly, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DRTSCIS, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: SLOOS net stronger demand, C&I, large and middle-market firms
terms.popup: Share of banks seeing stronger demand for business loans from big and mid-sized companies, net of those seeing weaker demand. Positive means companies want to borrow more.
terms.definition: Net Percentage of Domestic Banks Reporting Stronger Demand for Commercial and Industrial Loans From Large and Middle-Market Firms, from the SLOOS. Quarterly, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DRSDCILM, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: Delinquency rate on business loans, all commercial banks
terms.popup: Share of bank business loans that are behind on payments. A slow, lagging read on how the bank-lent middle market is coping.
terms.definition: Delinquency Rate on Business Loans, All Commercial Banks. From the Fed's Charge-Off and Delinquency Rates on Loans and Leases at Commercial Banks release. Quarterly, end of period, seasonally adjusted, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DRBLACBS, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: Net charge-off rate on business loans, all commercial banks
terms.popup: Share of bank business loans written off as lost, after any recoveries. The loss that finally lands, months after the delinquency shows up.
terms.definition: Charge-Off Rate on Business Loans, All Commercial Banks. Charge-offs are annualized and net of recoveries. Quarterly, seasonally adjusted, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CORBLACBS, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: Commercial and industrial loans, all commercial banks
terms.popup: Total business loans on US bank balance sheets, in billions of dollars. The size of the bank channel that private credit competes with.
terms.definition: Commercial and Industrial Loans, All Commercial Banks, from the Fed's H.8 release. Monthly, seasonally adjusted, billions of US dollars.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BUSLOANS, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index
terms.popup: A weekly gauge of how easy or hard it is to get money in US markets. Zero is average; above zero is tighter than normal, below zero is looser.
terms.definition: Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index. A weekly composite of US financial conditions across money markets, debt and equity markets, and the traditional and 'shadow' banking systems. Positive values mean tighter-than-average conditions, negative values looser. Weekly, ending Friday, index.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NFCI, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.expansion: St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index, version 4
terms.popup: A weekly stress gauge built from 18 market series. Zero is normal; above zero means more stress than usual, below zero less.
terms.definition: St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index, version 4. Built from 18 weekly series (seven interest rates, six yield spreads, five other indicators) whose average since late 1993 is set to zero; values above zero mean above-average stress. Version 4 replaced the backward-looking 90-day SOFR average with the forward-looking 90-day SOFR in two spreads. Weekly, ending Friday, index.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/STLFSI4, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.popup: The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year. Negative (inverted) has preceded most US recessions; positive is the normal shape.
terms.definition: 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity. Computed by the St. Louis Fed from the Treasury Department's constant-maturity yields. Daily, percent.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.popup: The prime rate: the base rate most US banks post for their best business customers. Small-business and revolving loans are often priced off it.
terms.definition: Bank Prime Loan Rate. The rate posted by a majority of the top 25 insured US-chartered commercial banks by domestic assets; one of several base rates banks use to price short-term business loans. Daily, percent, from the H.15 release.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DPRIME, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11

terms.popup: The yield on a 10-year US Treasury. The risk-free anchor that every credit spread on this page is measured against.
terms.definition: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis. From the Fed's H.15 release using the Treasury yield-curve methodology. Daily, percent. Read through the site's macro feed, not fetched twice.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Secondary tile; shared with the macro page

terms.popup: The yield on a 2-year US Treasury. It tracks where the market thinks the Fed's policy rate is heading over the next two years.
terms.definition: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 2-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis. From the H.15 release. Daily, percent. Read through the site's macro feed.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS2, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Secondary tile; shared with the macro page

terms.expansion: H.8 loans to nondepository financial institutions
terms.popup: Bank loans to non-bank lenders such as private credit funds and BDCs. It shows how much of private credit is itself funded by the banks.
terms.definition: Other Loans and Leases: Loans to Nondepository Financial Institutions, All Commercial Banks, from the H.8 release. Weekly, seasonally adjusted, billions of US dollars, from January 2015 ($2,031B on 2026-08-26). Shown as a level and as a share of TOTBKCR (10.1% at Jun 30 2026 vs 3.5% in June 2016), which reproduces PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives figure 101.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/LNFACBW027SBOG, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figure 101)
terms.whereUsed: Secondary tile 'share of bank credit'; benchmark row 'Bank loans to nondepository financial institutions'

terms.expansion: Total bank credit, all commercial banks
terms.popup: Total bank credit: all loans and securities held by US commercial banks. The denominator for the 'share of bank credit' tile.
terms.definition: Bank Credit, All Commercial Banks, from the H.8 release. Weekly, ending Wednesday, seasonally adjusted, billions of US dollars. This site labels the ratio LNFACBW027SBOG / TOTBKCR 'share of bank credit', never 'share of bank assets' (the share of total assets, TLAACBM027SBOG, is a different, smaller number).
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/TOTBKCR, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Denominator of the H.8 share tile

terms.popup: A 1/0 flag for recession months: from the month after the NBER peak through the trough. The dashboard shades those months gray on every long chart so you can see how a series behaved in past downturns.
terms.definition: NBER based Recession Indicators for the United States from the Period following the Peak through the Trough. Monthly dummy: 1 in a recession, 0 in an expansion; the recession begins the first day of the period after an NBER peak and ends the last day of the trough period. FRED offers three shading conventions; the St. Louis Fed uses the midpoint method in its own publications. FRED's trough method dates each recession from the month after the NBER peak through the trough month, which is how the bands on this page are drawn; the Strategy page's hand-keyed bands start at the peak month.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/USREC, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: Recession shading on M2, M3 and the long-run BAA10Y and DRTSCILM charts

terms.popup: Option-adjusted spread: the extra yield a bond pays over Treasuries after allowing for any call option, in basis points. Five of the six ICE BofA tiles here are OAS; the sixth is an effective yield.
terms.definition: The spread between a bond's yield and a spot Treasury curve, adjusted for embedded options such as the issuer's right to call the bond early. ICE BofA computes an OAS for each bond and weights them by market capitalization into an index OAS. Five of the six BAML* tiles on the Market view are OAS series; BAMLH0A0HYM2EY is an effective yield.
terms.source: ICE definition as given in the FRED Notes for BAMLH0A0HYM2 and BAMLH0A1HYBB (fetched 2026-09-11)
terms.whereUsed: All six ICE BofA tiles; M1 ladder subtitle 'OAS over Treasuries for bonds'
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter: refuter: five OAS tiles plus one effective-yield tile; the call-option sentence is a standard definition, not FRED wording; PR B: definition edited (Five of the six BAML* tiles on the Marke...)

terms.popup: The extra yield a bond pays over Treasuries after allowing for any call option, in basis points. Five of the six ICE BofA tiles here are OAS; the sixth is an effective yield.
terms.definition: Same as OAS.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A0HYM2
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.popup: The total yield a bond index pays, Treasury rate plus spread, weighted by market value. For high yield it is the going rate on a liquid alternative to a private loan.
terms.definition: The yield of an ICE BofA index computed from its capitalization-weighted constituents (ICE BofA's construction methodology). On this page it is BAMLH0A0HYM2EY, compared with the BDC composite yield and SOFR in the M2 yield stack.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A0HYM2EY (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: The floating reference rate a loan is priced over. Today that is SOFR for dollar loans (SONIA for sterling, EURIBOR for euro); the lender's margin is added on top.
terms.definition: The benchmark component of a floating-rate loan's coupon, reset periodically; the loan's all-in rate is base rate plus spread, subject to any floor. BDC books carry SOFR, SONIA and EURIBOR loans, so the dashboard says 'bps over base', never 'SOFR +'. The Fed's own note on DPRIME calls prime 'one of several base rates used by banks to price short-term business loans'.
terms.source: FRED Notes for DPRIME
terms.whereUsed: Every spread tile and bucket; M4 spread distribution

terms.popup: A minimum level for the base rate written into a loan. If SOFR falls below the floor, the borrower still pays the floor plus spread, so lenders keep income when rates drop.
terms.definition: A contractual lower bound on the reference rate used to compute a floating-rate loan's coupon. LCD's new-issue statistics report spread, floor and OID together. Floors are not captured in the 'spread over base' metric, which is a caveat on that popup.
terms.source: Usage: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026 (the 'Floor (bps)' column). Definition is standard.
terms.whereUsed: New-issue statistics; caveat on the spread-over-base popup

terms.popup: Original issue discount: the loan is sold below face value, say at 99 instead of 100. The discount is extra return to the lender on top of the spread, paid up front.
terms.definition: The difference between a loan's face value and the price at which it is issued, expressed in points; part of the all-in yield to the lender alongside spread, floor and fees. LCD reports OID with spread and floor in its new-issue statistics. Not captured in the spread-over-base metric.
terms.source: Usage: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026. Definition is standard.

terms.popup: A loan's spread over the base rate if held to maturity, counting the discount and fees as well as the coupon margin. The loan-market cousin of a bond's OAS.
terms.definition: The margin over the benchmark rate implied by a loan's price, coupon and maturity; LCD reports it for the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index (2000-2026 median 468 bps, figure 94) and for B-rated loans (median since 1997 4.8%, figure 53). Yield to maturity minus benchmark rate equals spread to maturity in figure 52.
terms.source: PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figures 52-53 and 94)
terms.whereUsed: M1 ladder long-run anchor (468 bps); the loan side of figure 94

terms.popup: The total annual return a loan or bond pays if held to maturity at today's price. For a floating-rate loan it is the base rate plus the spread to maturity.
terms.definition: The internal rate of return of a debt instrument's remaining cash flows at its current price. PitchBook's figure 52 attributes B-rated loan yield to maturity to a benchmark rate plus spread to maturity. LCD's playbook reports a primary-market YTM for new issues.
terms.source: PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figure 52); PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026

terms.popup: What a loan actually pays: base rate plus spread, after any floor. LCD's BDC chart tracks the cost-weighted average all-in interest rate on loans BDCs hold.
terms.definition: Base rate plus contractual spread, subject to the floor; excludes OID and fees. LCD slide 33: 'Cost-weighted average all-in interest rate (%)', 8.3% in Q2 2026, the lowest in four years. The dashboard treats all-in yield and spread over base as two separate metrics.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 33 title and chartHeading
terms.whereUsed: BDC composite all-in yield; M2 dot per quarter

terms.popup: The lender's margin over the floating base rate, in basis points. It is the price of credit risk plus illiquidity on a private loan, before floors, discounts and fees.
terms.definition: The contractual margin over SOFR, SONIA or EURIBOR. Computed for the BDC composite as cost-weighted InvestmentBasisSpreadVariableRate on floating debt, and shown as a distribution in 50 bps buckets. Caveats: floors, OID and fees are excluded; from 2026 LCD mixes privately sourced spreads with public ones; LCD's BDC buckets are by count.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 13 footnote
terms.whereUsed: M1 composite bar; M4 spread distribution

terms.popup: Basis points. One basis point is one hundredth of a percent, so 500 bps is 5.00%. Spreads are quoted in bps.
terms.definition: 1 bp = 0.01 percentage point. Every spread on the Market view is in bps; FRED serves the ICE series in percent, which the page multiplies by 100.
terms.source: Standard definition; not defined in the study material or on a fetched page

terms.popup: The extra yield on risky debt over a risk-free rate. Wider spreads mean investors want more pay for the risk; tighter spreads mean they are relaxed.
terms.definition: The yield difference between a corporate bond or loan and a Treasury or benchmark rate of the same maturity. Figure 94 of the Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives plots the ICE BofA HY OAS against the loan index spread-to-maturity and notes the two decoupled in 2026.
terms.source: PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights

terms.popup: Broadly syndicated loan: a large loan arranged by a bank and sold in pieces to many investors, mainly CLOs. It trades, it is rated, and it is the public rival to direct lending.
terms.definition: A leveraged loan underwritten by one or more arranging banks and syndicated to institutional investors, with a secondary market and ratings. LCD's BSL spread data 'reflects loans issued to borrowers rated B-minus' (slide 14) or 'to all leveraged borrowers' (slides 15-16). The MFA/Proskauer paper sizes the US institutional syndicated loan market at about $1.3 trillion (2022).
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 14-16 footnotes; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: See BSL. A bank-arranged loan sold to many lenders and traded afterwards, as opposed to a direct loan held by one lender or a small club.
terms.definition: Same as BSL.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43 methodology (direct lending 'not broadly syndicated')

terms.popup: The part of the syndicated loan market bought by funds and CLOs rather than banks: floating-rate term loans, mostly cov-lite, non-amortizing, and tradeable.
terms.definition: The institutional tranche of the leveraged loan market (term loan B and similar), as tracked by the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index. The MFA/Proskauer paper: cov-lite loans were 91% of the institutional loan market at Oct 4 2021, and most syndicated loans are non-amortizing.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Term loan B: the standard institutional leveraged loan. Floating rate, five to seven years, little or no scheduled repayment, sold to CLOs and loan funds.
terms.definition: A term loan tranche structured for institutional investors rather than banks, usually with nominal amortization and a bullet at maturity. LCD's daily playbook lists secondary prices and new issues by 'Term Loan B' and 'TLB Ext' (an extended TLB).
terms.source: Usage: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026. Definition is standard.

terms.popup: A loan to a company that already carries a lot of debt or is rated below investment grade. Floating rate and usually secured. Both BSL and direct loans are leveraged loans.
terms.definition: A syndicated or privately placed loan to a below-investment-grade or highly indebted borrower, typically floating rate and senior secured. The MFA/Proskauer paper cites $1.3 trillion of outstanding US leveraged loans in the S&P/LSTA index (2021-22).
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets. General definition is standard.

terms.expansion: Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index
terms.popup: The Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index, which tracks prices and returns of institutional loans. PitchBook uses it as the public stand-in for private debt returns.
terms.definition: A market-value-weighted index of US institutional leveraged loans that reports total return split into interest return and market return (figure 95), default rates by issuer count and by amount, and spread-to-maturity. PitchBook's 2024 report calls it 'a good proxy for private debt returns, particularly direct lending' (11.1% gross return, 12 months to Q2 2024).
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figures 94-95); PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.whereUsed: Default-rate and distressed-ratio references; the public return proxy

terms.expansion: Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan 100 Index
terms.popup: The Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan 100, an index of the 100 largest loans. Quoted as an average price: 100 is par, so 97.62 means loans trade at a small discount.
terms.definition: A sub-index of the leveraged loan index made up of the 100 largest facilities, quoted daily as a weighted average bid price. LCD's Sep 10 2026 playbook: 'The Morningstar LSTA US LL100 was the same to close at 97.62.' The Lenders view compares the BDC book mark (FV/cost) with it.
terms.source: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026. Index composition is a standard definition.

terms.popup: Collateralized loan obligation: a fund that buys hundreds of leveraged loans and pays for them by selling rated bonds in layers. CLOs are the biggest buyers of syndicated loans.
terms.definition: A securitization vehicle that holds a portfolio of leveraged loans and issues tranches of debt and equity against it. The MFA/Proskauer paper counts CLO securities within the US private credit market alongside BDCs and closed-end direct lending funds. LCD tracks US private credit / middle market CLO issuance (slide 37).
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 37

terms.popup: A CLO that holds directly originated middle-market loans instead of syndicated ones. It is how direct lenders borrow against their own loan books.
terms.definition: A private credit CLO whose collateral is directly originated, typically unrated middle-market loans, often managed by the originating lender. LCD slide 37: 'US private credit/middle market CLO issuance ($B)', count and volume rebounded slightly from Q2 2026.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 37 title and chartHeading
terms.whereUsed: Slide 37 series on the capital panel

terms.popup: A loan being made now, at today's terms, as opposed to one already outstanding and trading. New-issue spreads show where the market is pricing risk this month.
terms.definition: Primary-market transactions. LCD's methodology: 'Unless otherwise noted, data reflects new-issue direct lending transactions as tracked by PitchBook LCD.' Spread distributions on slides 13-19 are new-issue.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43 methodology

terms.popup: Where existing loans and bonds change hands after issue. Syndicated loans trade here; direct loans generally do not.
terms.definition: Trading of outstanding instruments between investors. LCD: unlike broadly syndicated loans, direct loans 'are generally not tradeable'; lenders intend to hold to maturity. The playbook's 'Secondary' section reports loan price moves.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43; PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026

terms.popup: When a borrower repays a loan from one market by raising a new one in the other: a private loan refinanced by a syndicated loan, or the reverse.
terms.definition: A refinancing that moves a borrower between the direct lending and BSL markets. LCD slides 38-41 track 'Syndicated loans and direct lending takeouts ($B)' and list recent loans in each direction; direct lending refinanced by BSL 'jumps sharply higher from Q2 levels'. The dashboard's M3 reading: BSL reopens and takeouts flow the other way.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 38-41 titles and chartHeadings
terms.whereUsed: Takeout series on the capital panel; M3 reading

terms.popup: Replacing an existing loan with a new one, usually to cut the rate, push out the maturity or change lenders.
terms.definition: Repayment of outstanding debt with new debt. PitchBook's 2024 report attributes lighter carry to 'a record year for repricings and refinancings'. LCD's playbook reports the volume of loans refinancing direct-lender debt.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 39-41

terms.popup: A borrower asking existing lenders to cut the spread on a loan, without new money, because the market has tightened. Common when loans trade above par.
terms.definition: An amendment that lowers the margin on an outstanding loan, typically when secondary prices are at or above par so lenders accept a lower coupon rather than be repaid. LCD's Sep 10 2026 playbook notes 'deadlines for several repricings'.
terms.source: Usage: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026; PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report. Definition is standard.

terms.popup: Lenders agree to push a loan's maturity out, usually for a higher spread or a fee, instead of the borrower refinancing. It moves a loan on the maturity wall without repaying it.
terms.definition: An amendment extending the maturity of an existing facility, often with a coupon step-up; a way to avoid refinancing in a tight market. LCD's playbook: 'the Sophos amend-and-extend transaction will officially launch'; 164 amendments year to date. The maturity-wall caveat: 'extensions move loans without repaying them'.
terms.source: Usage: PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026. Definition is standard.

terms.popup: The traditional default: a missed interest or principal payment, or a bankruptcy filing.
terms.definition: LCD's legacy default criteria: missed payments and bankruptcy filings, measured as a trailing-twelve-month rate among performing companies in the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index. 2.05% by issuer count at end-2023.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: The share of loans in an index that defaulted over the past twelve months, by number of borrowers or by dollars outstanding.
terms.definition: LCD measures default rates as the TTM calculation of defaults among performing companies in the loan index, by issuer count or by amount. The playbook reports the rate by amount outstanding at 0.5% in September 2026. The dual-track version adds distressed exchanges.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report; PitchBook LCD US Leveraged Loan Daily Playbook, September 10, 2026

terms.popup: LCD's broader default measure: missed payments and bankruptcies plus distressed exchanges. It catches the quiet restructurings the traditional rate misses.
terms.definition: LCD's rate that includes payment defaults and distressed exchanges (out-of-court restructurings, exchanges and subpar buybacks), by issuer count, TTM, in the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index. 3.8% at end-2023 against 2.05% payment-only. Proprietary and dated on this site.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: A troubled borrower swaps its debt for new debt worth less, or buys it back cheaply, to avoid bankruptcy. Lenders take a haircut now to recover more than a court process would give.
terms.definition: An out-of-court restructuring, exchange or subpar buyback counted as a default under LCD's dual-track rate. Distressed exchanges were 10% of loan defaults in 2019 and 47% in 2023; sponsored companies drove 90% of them in 2023. About 25% of 2020 exchangers defaulted again within three years.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: The share of performing loans priced below 80 cents on the dollar. It is an early-warning gauge: loans get cheap before they default.
terms.definition: LCD defines the distressed ratio as the share of performing loans in the index priced below 80. It was 4.5% ($62.8B) at end-December 2023, down from a post-pandemic high of 7.4% ($103.4B) in December 2022.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: How much of a defaulted loan lenders eventually get back, as a share of face value. Fast, out-of-court fixes recover more than long bankruptcies.
terms.definition: The discounted value recovered by lenders after a default. LCD's July 2023 LossStats study: average discounted recovery of 79% for distressed exchanges, 60% for bankruptcies under six months, 53% under one year, 47% for one to three years. Cov-lite facilities recover less than term loans with maintenance covenants.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Buying the loans or bonds of a company already in trouble, at a deep discount, in the hope of a profit through a restructuring.
terms.definition: PitchBook: a strategy that generally involves purchasing securities or loans in the secondary market rather than new origination, often targeting the 'fulcrum' security, the most subordinated part of the capital stack to be repaid in a bankruptcy, which can trade at steep discounts.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: A loan with no financial maintenance covenant, so lenders cannot step in when performance slips. Most syndicated loans are cov-lite; almost no private loans are.
terms.definition: A loan without financial maintenance covenants. Per LCD, 91% of the institutional loan market at Oct 4 2021 (1% in 2001); 86% of $1.3T of outstanding US leveraged loans. Per Proskauer, 1% of private credit loans in 2021, all to borrowers with at least $50M of EBITDA. Cov-lite facilities recover less than covenanted term loans.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets
terms.whereUsed: Structure popups; BSL vs direct lending comparison

terms.popup: A promise tested every quarter, such as debt under a set multiple of earnings. Breaking it lets lenders get to the table early, before a small problem becomes a default.
terms.definition: A financial covenant the borrower must satisfy at each test date (typically a total leverage ratio; sometimes also a fixed charge coverage ratio), as opposed to an incurrence covenant tested only when the borrower acts. Proskauer: 99% of private credit loans have at least one, 21% have two or more; they let lenders address problems 'before they become a crisis'.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Leveraged buyout: a private equity firm buys a company using mostly borrowed money. LBO loans are the core product of both direct lending and the syndicated market.
terms.definition: An acquisition financed largely with debt secured on the acquired company, led by a private equity sponsor. LCD slides 9-10 and 13-19 track direct lending deals financing LBOs and their spread distributions; slides 21-22 compare LBO counts and volumes in BSL versus direct lending.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 9-10, 13-19, 21-22 titles; PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report ('Often used in LBO transactions')

terms.popup: A borrower owned by a private equity firm (the sponsor). Sponsors bring repeat business and can inject equity when a company stumbles, so lenders treat these loans differently.
terms.definition: A company whose equity is controlled by a private equity fund. LCD tracks sponsor-backed direct lending deal counts and volumes (slides 6-7, 23-24); PitchBook shows PE-backed companies with lower payment default rates than nonsponsored ones, and sponsors driving 90% of 2023 distressed exchanges.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 6-7, 23-24; PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: What a loan is for. LCD's categories on slide 8 are LBO/M&A, refinancing, recapitalization (which includes dividend recaps) and other.
terms.definition: The stated purpose of a new loan. LCD slide 8: 'Count of PE-backed direct lending deals by use of proceeds', with the latest three months led by LBO and M&A activity.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 8 title and chartHeading
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.popup: One loan that does the job of senior and junior debt together, with a single blended rate. It is the standard private-credit structure; about nine in ten private loans are unitranches.
terms.definition: A senior secured facility that combines what would otherwise be first-lien and second-lien or mezzanine tranches under a single umbrella. Proskauer: 91% of private credit loans are unitranches; they may attach at 6.0x-7.0x EBITDA where a bank lends at 4.5x-5.0x, and typically carry a 50-100 bps premium over a syndicated first-lien loan. PitchBook: 'Unitranche facilities, which combine different debt instruments under a single umbrella, are also becoming more common.'
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets; PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.whereUsed: Slide 28 unitranche spread series; structure popups

terms.popup: The most senior secured loan: first claim on the borrower's assets if things go wrong. Lowest risk in the capital stack, so lowest spread.
terms.definition: Debt secured by a first-priority security interest in the borrower's collateral, repaid before second-lien, unsecured and equity claims. LCD's direct lending spread data 'reflects senior secured first-lien loans and unitranche facilities'; slide 29 tracks spreads on senior secured first-lien term loans held by BDCs.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 14 footnote and slide 29 chartHeading

terms.popup: A secured loan that ranks behind the first lien. It is repaid only after first-lien lenders, so it pays a higher spread and takes losses sooner.
terms.definition: Debt secured by a second-priority claim on the same collateral as the first lien. PitchBook includes second-lien loans within direct lending; Proskauer lists secured second lien among the minority of private credit loans that are not unitranches.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Inside a unitranche, the slice that gets paid last. Lenders privately split one loan into first-out and last-out pieces; the last-out piece earns more of the blended rate.
terms.definition: In a unitranche with an agreement among lenders, the tranche that is subordinated in payment priority to the first-out tranche in a workout, in exchange for a larger share of the interest. Tagged in BDC schedules of investments as 'first lien, last-out'.
terms.source: Standard definition; not defined in the study material or on a fetched page; unitranche context from MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: A bank underwriting a loan and then selling it down to many investors. The price can 'flex' up if buyers are scarce, which is the uncertainty direct lenders remove.
terms.definition: The process by which an arranging bank distributes a loan to institutional investors, subject to market flex on pricing and terms, with the risk of a 'busted' syndication. Private credit lenders instead commit to the entire loan without sell-down, and are paid for that certainty of execution.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: A loan made by a small group of direct lenders, typically one to five, who each hold their piece to maturity instead of selling it on.
terms.definition: LCD: direct lending 'is typically provided by a non-bank lender, or a small club, or group, of lenders'. Proskauer: most private credit loans are made by a single or small club of one to five lenders who are the company's largest and most senior creditors.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Loans made straight to a company by a non-bank lender, without a bank arranging or syndicating them. Usually senior, secured, floating rate and held to maturity.
terms.definition: LCD: 'directly originated loans to corporate borrowers that are not broadly syndicated', typically to unrated small to midsized companies, provided by a non-bank lender or a small club, generally not tradeable and held to maturity. PitchBook: generally senior loans to middle-market companies without an intermediary, which may include revolvers, second-lien loans and unitranches. Direct lending was 60% of private debt fundraising in 2024 and global direct lending AUM reached $678.5B as of June 30, 2024.
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43 methodology; PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report ('Fund type definitions' and the AUM figure)
terms.whereUsed: Every LCD volume series; AUM tile
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited (global direct lending AUM reached $678.5...)

terms.popup: Lending by funds and other non-banks rather than by banks, to companies that are too small or too indebted for the public bond and syndicated loan markets.
terms.definition: MFA/Proskauer: credit extended by non-bank investors with limited involvement by banks, in the US mostly to non-public middle-market companies that are below investment grade or unrated and smaller than syndicated-loan borrowers. The US market (BDCs, CLO securities and closed-end direct lending funds) exceeded $1 trillion of AUM in 2022 (the MFA/Proskauer figure, not the 2024 report's) against about $1.3 trillion of institutional syndicated loans.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited (exceeded $1 trillion of AUM in 2022 (the...)

terms.popup: PitchBook's name for the fund universe: direct lending, mezzanine, distressed, special situations, real estate, infrastructure, venture and bridge debt funds. Used interchangeably with private credit.
terms.definition: The private-markets asset class of closed-end and evergreen funds that lend or buy debt, as classified by PitchBook's fund type definitions. Private debt institutional AUM exceeded $1.8 trillion as of June 30, 2024 with $566.8 billion of dry powder; $2.2 trillion including wealth and insurance vehicles (same date).
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited (exceeded $1.8 trillion as of June 30, 20...)

terms.popup: Subordinated debt that sits between senior loans and equity, often with warrants or other equity kickers. Higher rate, repaid after the senior lender.
terms.definition: PitchBook: 'Subordinated debt, generally with features similar to preferred equity, such as warrants. Often used in LBO transactions.' Proskauer lists mezzanine (secured and unsecured) among private credit loans that are not unitranches; the industry began as mezzanine finance for the lower middle market.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: Opportunistic lending or structured equity, such as convertible debt or debt with warrants, made to gain influence or control over a company that is usually in some distress.
terms.definition: PitchBook: 'Opportunistic debt or structured equity investments, such as convertible debt, convertible preferred, and debt with warrants, made with the intent of gaining control of a company, generally one in some type of financial distress', through direct origination or secondary trading where prices are dislocated.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: Asset-based finance: lending secured by pools of specific assets, such as consumer loans, leases, receivables or equipment, rather than by a company's cash flow.
terms.definition: Private credit strategies that lend against or buy portfolios of financial or hard assets (for example student loan portfolios). PitchBook's 2023 report describes managers 'increasingly taking aim at asset-backed finance (ABF)' as nonbanks take share from banks, citing KKR's $2.1B Asset-Based Finance Partners fund (2022) and Apollo's ABF franchise. The report uses 'asset-backed' and 'asset-based' interchangeably.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: Loans to venture-backed startups, used to extend runway to the next round or exit without giving up more equity.
terms.definition: PitchBook: 'Debt financing extended to companies with venture capital backing. For entrepreneurs, venture debt serves as a way to extend the runway to exit without further diluting ownership.' Relevant to BDCs such as HTGC and TRIN.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report

terms.popup: Money investors have committed to funds that has not yet been lent out. It is the industry's spending power, and a lot of it means pressure to do deals.
terms.definition: Capital committed by limited partners but not yet called or invested. PitchBook charts AUM as remaining value plus dry powder; private debt dry powder reached a record $566.8 billion as of June 30, 2024, 31.1% of total AUM. The Benchmarks table reports 'Dry Powder %' per peer group.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; PitchBook Benchmarks, All Benchmarks table (data as of 2025 Q4)
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited (private debt dry powder reached a record...)

terms.popup: PitchBook's older name for dry powder, usually shown by vintage year so you can see how old the uncalled money is.
terms.definition: Uncalled committed capital, stacked by fund vintage. The Q2 2020 Private Fund Strategies Report charts 'Private debt capital overhang ($B)' with 'Overhang by vintage'. Same quantity as dry powder.
terms.source: PitchBook Q2 2020 Private Fund Strategies Report; PitchBook Fund Benchmarks: Data and Methodology (September 29, 2025) ('undrawn commitments')

terms.popup: Assets under management: what a manager's funds hold, at current value, plus the dry powder still to be called.
terms.definition: For private funds PitchBook computes AUM as remaining value (net asset value of investments still held) plus dry powder. Global direct lending AUM was $678.5 billion as of June 30, 2024 (22.2% ten-year CAGR); private debt institutional AUM over $1.8 trillion at the same date.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited (Global direct lending AUM was $678.5 bil...)

terms.popup: Net asset value: assets minus liabilities, the book value of a fund or BDC. For a listed BDC, price divided by NAV tells you what the market thinks of the manager's marks.
terms.definition: The value of a fund's holdings less its debts, as marked by the manager at period end; 'remaining value' in PitchBook's AUM chart. PitchBook notes the push into perpetual-life vehicles with 'continuous net asset value (NAV)-based offerings'.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.whereUsed: Price-to-NAV popup; remaining-value component of AUM

terms.popup: New money committed to private debt funds in a period, counted when a fund closes. The fundraising tiles use PitchBook's fundraising-report series.
terms.definition: Capital raised by funds reaching a close in the period, by strategy and region. PitchBook: $197.1 billion of committed capital was raised by private debt funds in 2024, with direct lending 60% of the total. LCD slide 36: 'US private debt capital raised by type ($B)'.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 36

terms.popup: The year a fund made its first investment. Funds are compared against others of the same vintage because they faced the same market.
terms.definition: PitchBook Benchmarking Methodology: 'The year in which a fund makes its first investment by delivering capital to a project or company. When we cannot confirm the year of first investment, the year of the fund's final close is used as the vintage year, or we rely on information provided by the GP.'
terms.source: PitchBook Fund Benchmarks: Data and Methodology (September 29, 2025)
terms.whereUsed: Fund glossary; dry powder by vintage

terms.popup: The total investors have pledged to a fund, called down over time. Fund size is measured by it, and management fees are usually charged on it.
terms.definition: PitchBook: 'Fund size: The total amount of capital committed by the fund's limited partners.' The fee popup on this site warns never to compare a BDC's expense ratio with 2/20, 'which is charged on committed capital'.
terms.source: PitchBook Fund Benchmarks: Data and Methodology (September 29, 2025)

terms.popup: Trailing twelve months: the last four quarters added together, whatever the calendar year. PitchBook reports TTM inflows among the top seven US alternative asset managers.
terms.definition: A rolling one-year window ending at the latest observation. LCD's default rates are 'the TTM calculation of defaults among performing companies' in the loan index; PitchBook reports TTM inflows for the top wealth platforms.
terms.source: PitchBook 2023 Annual Global Private Debt Report; PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.popup: Year to date: from January 1 to the latest data point. LCD compares YTD deal counts and volumes with the same point last year.
terms.definition: The period from the start of the calendar year to the as-of date. LCD slide 5: 'YTD volume and deal count are tracking behind last year's pace'; slide 14 footnote: 'Blank YTD data reflects insufficient data points to form a meaningful average.'
terms.source: LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slides 5 and 14

terms.popup: How far a reading sits from its own average, in standard deviations. Zero is normal; plus 2 is unusually high, minus 2 unusually low. PitchBook colors its dashboards by it.
terms.definition: (value minus mean) divided by standard deviation over a stated window. PitchBook's Quantitative Perspectives shades tables by 'the relative Z-score over the past 10 years' and plots long- and short-term Z-scores against a linear trend and a 12-month exponential moving average. The dashboard prints one beside each FRED tile's percentile.
terms.source: PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights

terms.popup: Where today's value ranks against its own history: the 18th percentile means it has been lower only 18% of the time in the window shown on the tile.
terms.definition: The share of observations in the stated window at or below the current value. The dashboard computes it over observations dated within the last ten years (about 120 monthly or daily points, about 40 for quarterly series); the ICE BofA OAS tiles use a three-year window because FRED serves only three years, and say so.
terms.source: This site's own construction: the rank of the latest value among the observations dated within the window named on the tile
terms.fixNote: PR B: source edited (This site's own construction: the rank o...)

terms.popup: Gray bands marking US recessions on a chart. The strategy page uses a hard-coded list of three recessions since 2001; the credit page derives bands from FRED's USREC series so the long-run charts are covered.
terms.definition: Shading of NBER-dated recession months, from FRED's USREC indicator (1 in recession, 0 otherwise; the midpoint method is the St. Louis Fed's own). The Market view derives its bands from USREC, so they start the month after the NBER peak (FRED's trough method); the Strategy page's three hand-keyed bands start at the peak month.
terms.source: FRED series page https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/USREC, Notes block, fetched 2026-09-11
terms.whereUsed: M2, M3 and long-run spread charts
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.popup: The Fed's quarterly survey of senior loan officers on whether their banks are tightening or loosening lending terms and seeing more or less demand.
terms.definition: Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices. Provides qualitative and limited quantitative information on bank credit availability and loan demand, plus special topics; reported as net percentages of banks. Source of DRTSCILM, DRTSCIS and DRSDCILM.
terms.source: FRED Notes for DRTSCILM, DRTSCIS and DRSDCILM (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: In SLOOS, the share of banks tightening minus the share loosening (or stronger demand minus weaker). Zero means the two sides balance.
terms.definition: The survey's summary statistic: respondents reporting tighter standards less those reporting easier, as a percent of respondents. The tile reading rule: over 20 is tightening, under -10 is loosening.
terms.source: FRED series titles for DRTSCILM and DRSDCILM

terms.popup: Commercial and industrial loans: bank loans to businesses for operations and investment, as opposed to real estate or consumer loans.
terms.definition: The Fed's category for business loans in the H.8 release (BUSLOANS) and the SLOOS (DRTSCILM, DRTSCIS, DRSDCILM). The 'business loans' delinquency and charge-off series (DRBLACBS, CORBLACBS) cover the same book.
terms.source: FRED series titles for BUSLOANS, DRTSCILM, DRSDCILM (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: Nondepository financial institutions: lenders that are not banks, such as private credit funds, BDCs, finance companies and mortgage companies. Banks increasingly lend to them.
terms.definition: The H.8 category 'loans to nondepository financial institutions' (LNFACBW027SBOG). PitchBook figure 101: bank exposure to NDFIs 'has expanded rapidly, now accounting for a larger share of commercial bank assets than consumer loans'. The MFA/Proskauer paper uses the related term NBFI (non-bank financial intermediaries).
terms.source: FRED series title for LNFACBW027SBOG; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights; MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets

terms.popup: The Fed's weekly statistical release on what US commercial banks hold: loans by type, securities and total bank credit.
terms.definition: H.8 Assets and Liabilities of Commercial Banks in the United States, the Federal Reserve Board release that sources BUSLOANS, LNFACBW027SBOG and TOTBKCR. Weekly (Wednesday) and monthly series, seasonally adjusted.
terms.source: FRED Notes 'Release' field for BUSLOANS, LNFACBW027SBOG and TOTBKCR (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: The Fed's daily release of selected interest rates: Treasury yields, the prime rate and other benchmarks.
terms.definition: H.15 Selected Interest Rates, the Federal Reserve Board release that sources DGS10, DGS2 and DPRIME; Treasury constant-maturity yields follow the Treasury yield-curve methodology.
terms.source: FRED Notes 'Release' field for DGS10, DGS2 and DPRIME (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: A Treasury yield read off the fitted yield curve at an exact maturity, such as ten years, rather than from one specific bond.
terms.definition: The Treasury Department's constant-maturity yields interpolate the daily yield curve at fixed tenors; used in DGS10, DGS2, T10Y2Y and BAA10Y.
terms.source: FRED series titles and Notes for DGS10, DGS2, T10Y2Y, BAA10Y (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: A loan the bank has given up on and removed from its books as a loss, net of anything later recovered.
terms.definition: The Fed's charge-off rate is annualized and net of recoveries (CORBLACBS). It lags delinquency because a loan must fall behind before it is written off.
terms.source: FRED Notes for CORBLACBS (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: A loan that is behind on a scheduled payment but not yet written off. The first visible sign of borrower stress in bank data.
terms.definition: The Fed's delinquency rate on business loans (DRBLACBS), quarterly, end of period, seasonally adjusted. Used as the lagging default proxy for the bank-lent middle market.
terms.source: FRED series title for DRBLACBS

terms.popup: High yield, or junk: bonds rated below investment grade (BB+ and lower). They pay more because the issuers are more likely to default.
terms.definition: Below-investment-grade corporate debt. ICE BofA's US High Yield Index includes bonds rated BB or below on an average of Moody's, S&P and Fitch, with an investment-grade country of risk, more than one year to maturity, fixed coupon and at least $100 million outstanding.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A0HYM2 (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: Investment grade: bonds rated BBB- or better. The safest corporate debt, and the cheapest for issuers.
terms.definition: Corporate debt rated BBB or better on an average of Moody's, S&P and Fitch. ICE BofA's US Corporate Index requires an investment-grade rating and country of risk, more than one year to maturity, fixed coupon and at least $250 million outstanding.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLC0A0CM (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: The top rung of high yield, one notch below investment grade. Solid companies with more debt than an IG rating allows.
terms.definition: The BB rating band (BB+, BB, BB-) on the S&P and Fitch scales, Ba on Moody's; the ICE BofA BB index is the BB-rated subset of the US High Yield Master II. Most direct-lending borrowers sit below this band or are unrated.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A1HYBB (fetched 2026-09-11); rating-scale mapping is standard

terms.popup: Single-B: the middle of high yield and the typical rating of a leveraged-buyout borrower. LCD's BSL comparisons often use B-minus loans.
terms.definition: The B rating band (B+, B, B-) on S&P and Fitch, B1-B3 on Moody's; the ICE BofA Single-B index is the B-rated subset of the US High Yield Master II. LCD slide 14 compares direct lending spreads with BSL loans to B-minus borrowers; PitchBook figures 52-53 track B-rated loan yields.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A2HYB; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 14 footnote; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights; rating-scale mapping is standard

terms.popup: The bottom of the rating scale before default. CCC borrowers depend on good conditions to keep paying, so their spreads swing hardest.
terms.definition: The CCC and lower bands (CCC+ to C) on S&P and Fitch, Caa-C on Moody's; the ICE BofA CCC & Lower index is that subset of the US High Yield Master II.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A3HYC (fetched 2026-09-11); rating-scale mapping is standard

terms.popup: Moody's lowest investment-grade band, equal to BBB at S&P and Fitch. The Baa bond yield is the classic gauge of borrowing costs for an average large company.
terms.definition: Moody's rating band Baa1-Baa3, the bottom of investment grade. Moody's Seasoned Baa Corporate Bond Yield (DBAA) less the 10-year Treasury yield is the BAA10Y series.
terms.source: FRED Notes for BAA10Y (fetched 2026-09-11); rating-scale mapping is standard

terms.popup: A credit agency's letter grade for how likely a borrower is to repay. AAA to BBB- is investment grade; BB+ and below is high yield.
terms.definition: An opinion on creditworthiness from Moody's, S&P or Fitch. ICE BofA assigns index membership on an average of the three. LCD notes direct-lending borrowers 'are typically unrated'.
terms.source: ICE definition via FRED Notes for BAMLH0A0HYM2; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43

terms.popup: The slope of the Treasury curve: 10-year yield minus 2-year. Below zero the curve is inverted, which has come before most US recessions.
terms.definition: The T10Y2Y spread, computed by the St. Louis Fed from Treasury constant-maturity yields. Daily, percent. Shown on the secondary conditions tile.
terms.source: FRED Notes for T10Y2Y (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: A composite that turns many rates and spreads into one number for how stressed markets are. The St. Louis Fed's version is zero on average; above zero is more stress than usual.
terms.definition: The St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index (STLFSI4) built from 18 weekly series; the Chicago Fed's NFCI is a related conditions index. Both are weekly and mean zero by construction.
terms.source: FRED Notes for STLFSI4 and NFCI (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: The base rate US banks post for their best business customers. Small-business loans and revolvers are often priced off it rather than SOFR.
terms.definition: Bank Prime Loan Rate (DPRIME): the rate posted by a majority of the top 25 US-chartered commercial banks; one of several base rates for short-term business loans.
terms.source: FRED Notes for DPRIME (fetched 2026-09-11)

terms.popup: The income a loan earns just from its coupon, as opposed to gains or losses from price moves. For floating-rate loans, carry rises and falls with the base rate.
terms.definition: The interest component of total return. PitchBook: 'carry remained the key driver of leveraged loan returns' in 2024 but lighter than 2023 after repricings and base-rate cuts; figure 95 splits the loan index return into interest return and market return. The yield-stack reading on this site: 'the interest component was 73.2% of the loan index gain'.
terms.source: PitchBook 2024 Annual Global Private Debt Report; PitchBook Q3 2026 Quantitative Perspectives: US Market Insights (figure 95)

terms.popup: Companies too small for the public bond and syndicated loan markets. The core private-credit borrower, usually unrated and often owned by a private equity sponsor.
terms.definition: The segment of non-public companies below investment grade or unrated and typically smaller than syndicated-loan borrowers (MFA/Proskauer); LCD adds that larger borrowers have also used direct lending in recent years. SLOOS splits C&I standards into 'large and middle-market firms' and 'small firms'.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets; LCD US Private Credit Monitor, August 2026, slide 43; FRED series title for DRTSCILM

terms.popup: The leverage, in turns of EBITDA, at which a loan's exposure sits. A unitranche that goes to 6 to 7x EBITDA is hit sooner than a bank loan that stops at 4.5 to 5x, because the company's value has less room to fall.
terms.definition: The leverage level at which a tranche's claim begins. Proskauer: a bank may lend at 4.5x-5.0x EBITDA while a unitranche may attach at 6.0x-7.0x; the 2013 leveraged-lending guidance drew the line at 6.0x. Value deterioration is borne first by the sponsor's equity, then junior debt, then the senior secured unitranche.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets
terms.fixNote: popup replaced per the refuter

terms.popup: A listed lender that raises money from public shareholders and lends it to mid-sized private US companies. It files with the SEC like any public company and is regulated under the 1940 Act.
terms.definition: A closed-end investment company that has elected BDC status under the Investment Company Act of 1940. It must invest mainly in private or thinly traded US companies, make significant managerial assistance available to them, and it may borrow only within the Act's asset-coverage limit. Every BDC on the site is identified by an SEC file number starting 814-.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-2(a)(48) (law.cornell.edu, fetched 2026-09-11); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30, Note 1
terms.whereUsed: Lenders view: universe, scorecard, every BDC row

terms.popup: The legal form behind every lender on this page: a US closed-end fund that elected BDC status, lends mostly to private companies, offers them managerial help, and lives under the 1940 Act's leverage cap.
terms.definition: Defined in section 2(a)(48) of the 1940 Act as a closed-end company organized and headquartered in the United States that invests in the securities described in section 55(a) (mainly private and small public US issuers), makes significant managerial assistance available, and has elected BDC treatment under section 54. BXSL's own words: 'structured as an externally managed, non-diversified, closed-end management investment company' that 'elected to be regulated as a business development company'.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-2(a)(48) (law.cornell.edu); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30, Note 1; SEC BDC data set readme.htm (2026_07_bdc.zip, sec.gov), Scope: 'file number beginning with 814-'
terms.whereUsed: Lenders view header and universe note

terms.popup: The federal law that governs funds and BDCs. For a BDC it sets the borrowing limit (asset coverage), the rule against selling shares below NAV, and the definitions of control and affiliation.
terms.definition: The Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. §80a-1 et seq.). Sections used on this page: 18 (senior securities and asset coverage), 61 (BDC capital structure, the 200% and 150% tests), 63 (sales below net asset value), 2(a)(3) and 2(a)(9) (affiliated person and control).
terms.source: law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/80a-18, 80a-60, 80a-62, 80a-2 (fetched 2026-09-11); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30, Note 1

terms.popup: The 1940 Act's leverage test: (total assets − liabilities other than debt) ÷ debt. A BDC must stay at or above 150% (or 200%) to borrow more. BXSL was at 178% on June 30, 2026.
terms.definition: Section 18(h): the ratio of total assets less all liabilities not represented by senior securities to the aggregate amount of senior securities representing indebtedness. Section 61 sets the BDC minimum at 200%, or 150% after the 2018 election. Formula on this site: (total assets − liabilities not represented by senior securities) ÷ (senior debt − SBA debentures where the filer states exemptive relief); the tagged ratio InvestmentCompanySeniorSecurityIndebtednessAssetCoverageRatio where it exists. Filers also print it per $1,000 of debt in the senior-securities table.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-18(h) and §80a-60(a) (law.cornell.edu); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30
terms.whereUsed: Scorecard row Asset coverage; chart L3; composite strip

terms.popup: In the 1940 Act, a fund's debt and preferred stock: anything that ranks ahead of common shareholders. Asset coverage is measured against senior securities that are debt.
terms.definition: Section 18(g): any bond, debenture, note or similar obligation or instrument constituting a security and evidencing indebtedness, and any stock of a class having priority over any other class as to distribution of assets or payment of dividends. Excludes a promissory note issued for a loan 'made by a bank or other person and privately arranged, and not intended to be publicly distributed' in the cases the section lists. BXSL: '$7.6 billion ... of senior securities outstanding' at June 30, 2026.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-18(g) (law.cornell.edu); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30

terms.popup: Long-dated, government-guaranteed borrowings raised by a BDC's SBIC subsidiary. Filers with SEC relief leave them out of the asset-coverage test, so their ratio looks higher than the raw formula gives.
terms.definition: Debt issued by a wholly owned subsidiary licensed as a small business investment company under the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 and guaranteed by the SBA. Section 61(a) of the 1940 Act addresses a BDC's guarantee of such indebtedness; several BDCs hold SEC exemptive relief to exclude the debentures from the asset-coverage calculation (unconfirmed seed list, pending a filing sentence per name: MAIN, FDUS, CSWC, GAIN, GLAD, SAR, OFS; MAIN's 10-Q sentence 'our BDC asset coverage ratio was 244%' is the one confirmed so far).
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-60(a)(5) (law.cornell.edu, fetched 2026-09-11)
terms.workingRef: blueprint §4.2 Asset coverage row (sbaExempt seed and MAIN sentence)
terms.fixNote: PR B: definition edited ((unconfirmed seed list, pending a filing...)

terms.popup: An SEC order that lets a fund do something the 1940 Act would otherwise forbid: co-invest alongside sister funds, or leave SBA debentures out of the leverage test.
terms.definition: Relief granted by SEC order on application. Two kinds matter here: co-investment relief, which lets a BDC and other funds run by the same adviser share deals (the Act's general prohibition on joint transactions with affiliates), and relief that excludes SBA-guaranteed debentures from the asset-coverage calculation. The site records the second kind per filer as sbaExempt with the filing sentence as provenance.
terms.source: MFA and Proskauer, The Role of Private Credit in U.S. Capital Markets (the SEC-order discussion); the filer's own 10-Q sentence on SBA debentures

terms.popup: A BDC's borrowing limit is 200% asset coverage (1:1 debt to equity) unless its board or shareholders took the 2018 option to drop to 150% (about 2:1). 14 of the 19 exchange-listed BDCs tagging the ratio report under 200% (frames CY2026Q2I).
terms.definition: Section 61(a)(1) sets BDC asset coverage at 200%. Section 61(a)(2) lowers it to 150% if the company discloses the approval within five business days, reports senior securities and coverage in its periodic filings, and the change was approved either by a 'required majority' of directors (effective one year later) or by more than 50% of votes cast by shareholders (effective at once). BXSL's sole initial shareholder approved the 150% threshold on September 25, 2018. Filers that never elected stay at 200%; the site reads the 10-K to tell them apart. Of the 76 filers tagging the asset coverage ratio in SEC frames CY2026Q2I (fetched 2026-09-11), 19 are listed on the NYSE or Nasdaq and 14 of those report under 200%; the one OTC filer (FRBP, 1.78) is not counted.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-60(a)(1)-(2) (law.cornell.edu); BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30; SEC XBRL frames CY2026Q2I and the SEC submissions feed (exchange field), fetched 2026-09-11
terms.fixNote: PR B: popup edited (15 of the 19 listed BDCs tagging the rat...); PR B: popup edited (A BDC's borrowing limit is 200% asset co...)

terms.popup: How far the BDC sits above its legal leverage line: coverage ÷ 150% − 1. BXSL at 178% has an 18.7% cushion. Under 15% is the site's flag.
terms.definition: cushion = asset coverage ÷ statutory minimum − 1 (150% or 200% per the election). The companion figure is the portfolio markdown that would break the ratio, 1 − 150 ÷ coverage: 11.8% at 170%, 9.1% at 165%, 6.3% at 160%. Below the line a BDC cannot borrow and, while its public notes lack coverage, cannot pay a distribution or buy back stock (§18(a)(1)(B) via §61).

terms.popup: Net assets divided by shares outstanding. The number the share price is compared with. ARCC $19.35, BXSL $25.53, MAIN $33.92 at June 30, 2026.
terms.definition: XBRL tag NetAssetValuePerShare, unit USD per share (frames path segment USD-per-shares). Reported at every 10-Q and 10-K date; the site labels each value by calendar period end.
terms.source: us-gaap taxonomy element NetAssetValuePerShare, as tagged by every listed BDC on SEC EDGAR companyfacts

terms.popup: Share price ÷ NAV per share: the market's opinion of the manager's marks. Above 1.0× the BDC can grow by issuing stock; below 1.0× it needs a shareholder vote to do so.
terms.definition: Market close ÷ NetAssetValuePerShare, computed on the site (ARCC 19.63 ÷ 19.35 = 1.01×, BXSL 24.34 ÷ 25.53 = 0.95×, MAIN 56.16 ÷ 33.92 = 1.66× on 2026-09-10). The market feed's price-to-book is a different number and is never shown. Read against the sector median (0.80× in April 2026) and against 1.0×.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-62(2) (law.cornell.edu)

terms.popup: Price to NAV expressed as a gap: 1.05× is a 5% premium, 0.95× a 5% discount. A lasting discount says the market expects losses the book has not yet taken.
terms.definition: premium/discount = price ÷ NAV per share − 1. Shaded as a band on chart L1 with 1.0× drawn as the statutory line, because under section 63(2) a BDC may sell common stock below NAV only with shareholder approval within the prior year and a good-faith board determination.
terms.source: 15 U.S.C. §80a-62(2) (law.cornell.edu)

terms.popup: A BDC's earnings from interest and fees after its costs, before gains and losses on the loans. It is the cash-like profit that pays the dividend.
terms.definition: Investment income − operating expenses (management and incentive fees, interest, administration) − income and excise taxes, before realized and unrealized gains. XBRL: NetInvestmentIncome (often before tax) and InvestmentIncomeOperatingAfterExpenseAndTax (after tax). ARCC Q2 2026: $367M before, $359M after tax.
terms.source: BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30 (income definition used for the fee)
terms.workingRef: blueprint §4.2 NII row and §8 Net investment income

terms.popup: Interest, dividends and fees earned on the portfolio, minus the fund's expenses and taxes. Excludes any change in the value of the loans. Includes PIK income that has been accrued but not received in cash.
terms.definition: The GAAP subtotal on a BDC's statement of operations before net realized and unrealized gains. It includes accrued non-cash income such as PIK and OID accretion; a shortfall against the dividend is met from spillover, realized gains or capital, in that order of comfort. The fourth fiscal quarter is derived as the 10-K figure minus the three 10-Qs.
terms.source: BXSL 10-Q 2026-06-30 (the income-recognition and incentive-fee notes)

terms.popup: Net investment income after the fund's income and excise taxes. This is the GAAP figure and the one the press release quotes; some filers tag NII before tax, so the site records which line answered.
terms.definition: InvestmentIncomeOperatingAfterExpenseAndTax where tagged; else NetInvestmentIncome − InvestmentIncomeOperatingTaxExpenseBenefit; else NetInvestmentIncome labeled 'no tax line tagged'; else InvestmentIncomeNet. ARCC tags both ($367M before, $359M after $8M of tax, Q2 2026); BXSL $178.2M / $173.8M; MAIN $93.8M / $90.3M. Cross-check: NII ÷ weighted shares equals the per-share tag within a cent.
terms.source: us-gaap taxonomy elements InvestmentIncomeOperatingAfterExpenseAndTax, NetInvestmentIncome and InvestmentIncomeOperatingTaxExpenseBenefit on SEC EDGAR companyfacts (ARCC, BXSL and MAIN, Q2 2026)
terms.whereUsed: Scorecard; dividend coverage; NII return on NAV

terms.popup: A company-defined version of NII that strips out items the manager calls one-off (for ARCC, 'Core EPS'). Not GAAP, not computed here; shown only where the filing states it.
terms.definition: Adjusted or core net investment income per share as the filer defines it in its earnings release or 10-Q. Definitions differ by filer, so the site never computes it and shows the disclosed figure with the sentence as provenance.
terms.source: The BDC's own earnings release or 10-Q, where a core or adjusted NII is disclosed; this site's disclosed-only rule

terms.popup: MAIN's name for its adjusted NII: what it considers available to pay out ($1.04 per share, Q2 2026). Company-defined, shown only where stated.
terms.definition: A filer-defined non-GAAP measure of net investment income available for distribution, typically adding back non-cash compensation or excluding items the manager treats as unusual. Disclosed only, never derived.
terms.source: The BDC's own earnings release (MAIN Q2 2026: 'distributable NII' $1.04 per share); this site's disclosed-only rule

terms.popup: Taxable income a BDC earned but has not yet paid out, carried into the next year. It is a reserve that can top up the dividend when a quarter's NII falls short.
terms.definition: Income realized but not distributed in prior years, which the excise-tax test (98% of ordinary income, 98.2% of capital gain net income, plus prior undistributed amounts) requires to be paid out or taxed at 4%. Read from the 10-K tax note per share, with the sentence as provenance; blank otherwise. ARCC's board states it considers undistributed taxable income carried forward when setting dividends.

terms.popup: A 4% federal tax a BDC pays on income it keeps instead of distributing on time. Paying it is a choice: keep spillover and pay 4%, or pay everything out.
terms.definition: A nondeductible 4% federal excise tax on undistributed income unless the company distributes each year at least 98% of ordinary income, 98.2% of capital gain net income for the year to October 31, and any prior-year income realized but not distributed. BXSL accrued $4.4M in Q2 2026. It sits below NII in the after-tax line.
